newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaitis to vote in only Gulf Arab parliament poll.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaitis to vote in only Gulf Arab parliament poll.

text.p: Kuwaiti men will elect on Monday the only parliament in a Gulf Arab state in the second poll since Kuwait was freed in 1991 of Iraq's occupation.
Some 107,000 men, about a seventh of Kuwaiti nationals, are allowed to vote to pick 50 new MPs from 230 candidates seeking a seat in one of the Arab world's most vociferous parliaments.
Although most Kuwaitis do not have the right to vote Western diplomats say the process is unique by Gulf Arab standards.
Western allies who helped end Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait are privately pressing for female political rights.
"This is something we have pressed for...Unfinished business is votes for women," said a senior Western diplomat.
Kuwaiti women, about 50 percent of nationals, help to steer the oil industry, run businesses and head diplomatic missions but when Kuwaiti men vote on October 7, they won't take part.
They plan to hold a "silent march" on election day to demand political rights.
Military and police personnel, Kuwaitis naturalised less than two decades ago and citizens under 21 cannot vote either. Only Kuwaiti men born to Kuwaiti fathers can.

Western powers and Kuwaiti politcians urged the ruling al- Sabah family after the Gulf War to fulfil its pledge during the occupation to restore parliament which was dissolved in 1986 at the height of the nearby Iran-Iraq war.

Whatever the outcome of the vote, Kuwait's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah is expected to form a post-election government even if the new parliament is once again dominated by opposition MPs.

No political parties are officially allowed in Kuwait to avoid rifts in the sensitive social balance but almost every political ideology is represented in the election for the parliament which will take Kuwait into the next century.

The sharp-tongued chamber is no rubber stamp. It has taken painful bites out of government prestige throughout its 33 years of existence and in particular since the 1991 Gulf War, with tough probes into alleged corruption.
In the past "the executive ignored parliament. Now they do work together," said a Western diplomat. "They have found a capacity to understand each other or at least work together."
Many Western states are interested in the outcome of the vote and their diplomats are often seen at election rallies.

Parliament's Islamists, liberals and independents have made their presence felt wherever Kuwait does business -- from Europe, to Asia and North America -- by trying to closely monitor flows of public funds and defence deals.
Western diplomats now say the institutions of democracy in Kuwait are well established.
There are 25 constituencies in Kuwait with two parliament seats for each. The largest has 9,740 eligible voters and the smallest has 1,129.
